text:
The Great Molasses Flood

January 15, 1919, was unusually mild in Boston. A few days earlier the temperature had been close to zero. By midday it had risen above 40 degrees Fahrenheit, and people in the North End were out in their shirtsleeves. Laborers ate lunch near the waterfront, children collected firewood, and city workers stayed in their yard on Commercial Street.

Over the neighborhood stood a steel tank about 50 feet tall and 90 feet across. The Purity Distilling Company owned it, and it held about 2.3 million gallons of molasses. The molasses was waiting to be made into industrial alcohol, which went into munitions during the war that had just ended. Two days before, a ship had topped up the tank with a fresh load of warm molasses. That made it nearly full.

At about 12:30 p.m., witnesses heard a deep rumble and a series of sharp cracks that some said sounded like machine-gun fire. Those were the rivets popping out of the tank's seams. Then the tank split open.

A wave of molasses, by some accounts 25 feet high, poured into the narrow streets at an estimated 35 miles an hour. It knocked buildings off their foundations. It bent the steel girders of the elevated railway on Atlantic Avenue, and a train only just stopped in time. It caught people, horses, and wagons and carried them along. Molasses is heavy and thick. Anyone it knocked down struggled to stand up again, and as the cold afternoon air cooled it, it got thicker still. People who were trapped could not move, and some suffocated in the brown mass.

Rescuers came quickly. Sailors from the training ship USS Nantucket, which was docked nearby, ran in, followed by police, firefighters, and Red Cross volunteers. They waded through waist-deep syrup to pull out survivors. A makeshift hospital was set up close by. The search for bodies went on for days, and some victims were not found until months later. Twenty-one people died, among them a ten-year-old boy, and about 150 were injured.

Cleanup was miserable work. Crews sprayed salt water from fireboats to break down the molasses and shoveled sand over what was left. Rescuers and onlookers tracked the syrup across the city on their boots, so it ended up on streetcars, in telephone booths, and in houses miles away. For months the harbor was stained brown. For decades, longtime residents said the neighborhood smelled sweet on hot summer days.

The tank's owner, United States Industrial Alcohol, said anarchists had blown it up. The evidence pointed somewhere else. The tank had been built in a hurry in 1915 under the supervision of a company treasurer who had no engineering training. Nobody tested it properly by filling it with water. It leaked so badly from the beginning that the company painted it brown so the streaks wouldn't show, and neighbors collected the drips to use at home. More than a hundred families sued, and the case took years. In 1925 a court-appointed auditor found the company responsible. It paid about $628,000 in settlements.

The disaster changed building practice. Massachusetts, and later other states, began requiring licensed engineers to sign off on construction plans. Today the site on Commercial Street is a park with a baseball field and a bocce court. A small plaque records the day a tide of molasses swept through the North End.
